formation.title: The Rise of Bengal
formation.text:
The Bengal Sultanate has united the fertile Ganges delta under a single banner. From the great ports of Chittagong and Satgaon to the legendary weaving centers of Sonargaon and Dhaka, this land commands wealth that draws the envy of empires. Chinese admirals call it 'the richest country to trade with,' and Moroccan travelers marvel at its cloth. Now, at the moment of formation, a choice presents itself: shall Bengal pour its energies into the textile trade that makes it wealthy, or forge its armies and fleets into instruments of territorial expansion?

This choice unlocks a destiny path in the Traditions tab.

options.text: Let the looms weave our destiny.

modifiers.name: Looms of Sonargaon
modifiers.text: The finest cotton cloth in the world flows from Bengal's looms. Muslin so sheer it was called 'woven air' commands the markets of Asia and beyond, making Bengal the richest trading land in the subcontinent.

options.text: Our rivers shall carry armies, not just merchants.

modifiers.name: Sword of the Ganges
modifiers.text: Bengal's vast population, riverine geography, and war elephant tradition make it a formidable military power. The rivers serve as highways for armies, and the delta's bounty sustains campaigns that lesser realms could never mount.

advances.name: Delta Agriculture
advances.text: The art of managing the Ganges delta's annual floods (building earthen bunds, directing water through canals, and timing rice planting to the monsoon cycle) sustains one of the most densely populated regions on earth.

advances.name: Sultanate Divan
advances.text: The Bengal Sultanate's administrative council, the Divan, blends Central Asian governance traditions with local Bengali practices, creating a multicultural bureaucracy where Hindus and Muslims serve side by side.

advances.name: Muslin Tradition
advances.text:
Bengali weavers produce muslin so fine that travelers call it 'woven air.' The cloth of Sonargaon and Dhaka is prized from China to the Mediterranean, and the techniques are passed down through generations of master craftsmen.

Available in: Muslin Workshop

advances.name: River Flotilla
advances.text: In riverine Bengal, control of the waterways is control of the country. Shallow-draft galleys patrol the thousands of channels that crisscross the delta, providing both military security and commercial regulation.

advances.name: Iwaz Khalji's Naval Legacy
advances.text: Iwaz Khalji first organized a naval force in Islamic Bengal, recognizing that the river navy was of prime necessity in a land where waterways outnumber roads. His legacy shapes Bengal's military doctrine for centuries.

advances.name: Sonargaon Arong
advances.text: The arong, a marketplace where muslin is produced and sold, reaches its peak at Panam Nagar in Sonargaon. Here merchants from across Asia gather to bid on the finest cloth in the world.

advances.name: Hussain Shahi Court
advances.text: The Hussain Shahi dynasty presides over Bengal's golden age from the capital at Gaur. Under their patronage, Bengali literature, architecture, and administration reach unprecedented heights.

event.title: The Golden Age of the Hussain Shahis
event.text: Under the Hussain Shahi dynasty, Bengal enters its golden age. From the magnificent capital at Gaur, the sultanate's territories stretch from Arakan to Orissa, from Assam to Tripura. Hindus and Muslims serve together in the royal administration, poets compose in Bengali alongside Persian, and the architectural masterpieces of Gaur-Lakhnauti rise in distinctive brick and terracotta. This is a moment of extraordinary cultural flourishing, but also of military ambition. The Hussain Shahis have expanded Bengal's borders further than any previous dynasty. How shall this golden age be directed?

options.text: Patronize the arts and scholars of Bengal.

modifiers.name: Golden Age Patronage
modifiers.text: The Hussain Shahi court is a beacon of culture and learning, attracting poets, architects, and scholars from across the subcontinent.

options.text: Press our advantage and expand our borders.

modifiers.name: Golden Age Expansion
modifiers.text: The Hussain Shahi armies have pushed Bengal's borders to their greatest extent, establishing dominion over Arakan, Orissa, and beyond.

advances.name: War Boat Tradition
advances.text: Bengal's war boatmen, paik-backed infantry who fight from river craft, are the backbone of the monsoon-season military. Where cavalry fails in flooded terrain, these riverine warriors prevail.

advances.name: Adina Congregation
advances.text: The grand congregational mosques of Bengal, built in the distinctive local brick-and-terracotta tradition, serve as centers of both religious devotion and community life. The Adina Mosque at Pandua, modeled after the great mosques of Damascus and Ctesiphon, stands as the largest in the subcontinent.

advances.name: Bengali Coinage
advances.text: The Bengal Sultanate mints its own silver tankas, establishing financial independence from Delhi. This independent monetary system facilitates trade and attracts merchants to Bengal's markets.

advances.name: Chittagong Customs
advances.text: Chittagong, Bengal's premier seaport, handles the majority of overseas exports, fine muslins, indigo, rice, and spices flow outward while horses, bullion, and luxury goods pour in from across the Indian Ocean.

advances.name: Muslin Export
advances.text: Bengal's muslin trade reaches global proportions. Annual fleets of five or six ships carry textiles worth eighty to ninety thousand cruzados to Malacca alone, while European trading companies compete fiercely for access to Bengal's cloth. The ships are built and fitted out at Chittagong.

advances.name: River Patrol
advances.text: Fast patrol boats protect Bengal's vast river trade network from piracy and smuggling, ensuring that the wealth flowing through the delta's channels reaches the Nawab's treasury.

advances.name: Nawab Governance
advances.text: Bengal's Nawabs evolve a distinctive provincial administration that balances central authority with local autonomy, managing one of the most populous and productive regions in the world.

advances.name: Bay of Bengal Trade
advances.text: Bengal's maritime trade networks span the Bay of Bengal, connecting Chittagong and Satgaon to Burma, Malacca, the Maldives, Sri Lanka, and the ports of Southwest Asia and East Africa.

advances.name: Murshidabad Silk
advances.text:
Murshidabad's silk weavers produce golden brocades and kincabs that are prized across the Mughal world. The city's looms turn raw silk into fabric fit for emperors, establishing Bengal as a center of luxury textile production.

Available in: Muslin Workshop

advances.name: Revenue Reforms
advances.text: Systematic revenue assessment and collection transforms Bengal from a province prone to fiscal chaos into the financial backbone of the Mughal Empire, contributing more than half of all imperial revenue.

event.title: The Revenue Reforms of Murshid Quli Khan
event.text: Murshid Quli Khan, the first independent Nawab of Bengal, has transformed the province's administration. Moving the capital from Dhaka to the newly founded city of Murshidabad, he implements sweeping revenue reforms that systematize tax collection across Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. His mal zamini system assigns fixed revenue assessments to landholders, replacing the chaotic farming of taxes with an orderly bureaucracy. Bengal's treasury overflows, the province now contributes more than half of all Mughal imperial revenue. But this centralization comes at a cost to merchant autonomy. Shall the state tighten its grip on revenue, or allow the trading classes greater freedom?

options.text: Centralize revenue under the Nawab's authority.

modifiers.name: Revenue Centralization
modifiers.text: Murshid Quli Khan's mal zamini system has transformed Bengal into the most efficiently taxed province in the subcontinent.

options.text: Give the merchants freedom to grow our wealth.

modifiers.name: Merchant Freedom
modifiers.text: Bengal's merchants operate with unprecedented autonomy, their trading networks spanning the Bay of Bengal and beyond.

advances.name: Arsenal Tradition
advances.text: Bengal's arsenals manufacture gunpowder, saltpetre, and weaponry on an industrial scale. The province is one of the world's largest producers of saltpetre, a critical ingredient in gunpowder.

advances.name: Matchlock Infantry
advances.text: Bengali banduqchi, matchlock musketeers, combine the firearm traditions introduced from Central Asia with local military organization. They provide disciplined firepower in Bengal's increasingly gunpowder-dominated armies.

advances.name: Diplomatic Balance
advances.text: Bengal's geographic position and economic importance demand a sophisticated approach to diplomacy, balancing the ambitions of Mughal emperors, Arakanese kings, and European trading companies.

advances.name: Nawab Treasury
advances.text: The sarraf kothhi, banking houses, of Bengal manage the flow of revenue from the richest province in the Mughal Empire. Bengali bankers extend credit across the subcontinent, financing trade and government alike.

advances.name: Cotton Processing
advances.text:
Advances in cotton ginning and preparation improve the quality and quantity of raw material available to Bengal's legendary weavers, sustaining the textile industry that is the foundation of the province's wealth. Beside the fine muslins, plain piece goods are woven by the bale for the trading companies.

Available in: Muslin Workshop

advances.name: Sepoy Corps
advances.text: The Nawab's sepoy regiments represent the professionalization of Bengal's military. Trained in European drill and armed with modern muskets, these disciplined infantry are a formidable force, as both the Nawab's rivals and the East India Company discover.

advances.name: Delta Hydraulics
advances.text: Centuries of experience managing the Ganges delta's complex hydrology culminate in sophisticated water management systems that support dense settlement, intensive rice cultivation, and commercial navigation.

advances.name: Jute Industry
advances.text: Bengal becomes the world center of jute production and processing. The strong, flexible fiber (used for rope, sacking, and coarse textiles) becomes one of Bengal's most important export commodities in the industrial era.

advances.name: Bengali Renaissance
advances.text: An intellectual revolution transforms Bengali society. Writers, poets, and reformers create a new Bengali literature, establish modern educational institutions, and challenge social conventions, laying the groundwork for a modern national identity.

event.title: The Bengali Renaissance
event.text: A great intellectual awakening stirs in Bengal. Scholars, poets, and reformers are reimagining Bengali identity through literature, philosophy, and social criticism. The Bengali language itself becomes a vehicle for modernizing thought, as writers challenge old orthodoxies and envision a reformed society. Universities and printing presses multiply, literacy spreads beyond the traditional elite, and new ideas about governance and individual rights take root in the fertile soil of Bengal's intellectual tradition. This renaissance can follow two paths: a literary revolution that transforms hearts and minds, or a practical reform movement that reshapes institutions.

options.text: Let the written word illuminate Bengal.

modifiers.name: Literary Awakening
modifiers.text: The Bengali Renaissance has sparked an explosion of literature, scholarship, and new ideas that is transforming the intellectual landscape.

options.text: Reform our institutions for a new age.

modifiers.name: Reform Movement
modifiers.text: Bengali reformers are modernizing the province's institutions, creating a more efficient and responsive administration.

advances.name: Indigo Plantations
advances.text: Bengal's lowlands prove ideal for growing indigo, and the province becomes a major supplier of the prized blue dye to European textile manufacturers. Indigo vats dot the countryside, processing the plant into concentrated dye cakes for export.

advances.name: Bengali Movable Type
advances.text: In 1778 the smith Panchanan Karmakar cut the first movable type for the Bengali script at Hooghly, and a grammar of the language was printed with it. From 1800 he and his pupils cast type at Serampore for Bengali and a dozen other scripts. A language that had lived in manuscript and recitation can now be set, printed and sold by the thousand.

destiny.name: Destiny of Bengal
destiny.text: Bengal stands at the crossroads of its future. With formation complete, the nation must now decide the shape of its greatness, whether through the wealth of its legendary looms or the strength of its river-borne armies.

event.title: The Destiny of Bengal
event.text: Bengal has risen. What was once a collection of river principalities and sultanate provinces is now a unified power commanding the richest delta in the world. The monsoon winds carry trade from a hundred ports; the rivers nourish fields that feed millions. Now the question is not whether Bengal will be great, but how. Will its greatness be measured in bolts of cloth or lengths of steel?

destiny.name: Textile Hub of the East
destiny.text: Extend Bengal's textile dominance by seizing control of Masulipatnam on the Coromandel Coast and ensuring silk flows through the capital market. This establishes Bengal as the center of cloth production across the Indian Ocean.

conditions.text: Own Masulipatnam, or a subject owns it

children.text: Silk is produced in the market
Silk is traded in the market

event.title: The Textile Hub of the East
event.text: Bengal's looms now set the price of cloth from the Coromandel to the Straits. With Masulipatnam secured, the textile trade of the entire eastern coast flows through Bengali hands. Merchants from China, Persia, and the Mediterranean compete for access to our cotton and silk. The arongs of Sonargaon and the workshops of Dhaka hum with activity day and night.

options.text: The world clothes itself in our fabric.

destiny.name: Bay of Bengal Network
destiny.text: Project Bengali commercial power across the Bay of Bengal by securing Malacca and Martaban. These distant ports connect Bengal's textile exports to the spice trade of Southeast Asia and the overland routes of mainland Burma.

conditions.text: Own Malacca, or a subject owns it
Own Martaban, or a subject owns it

event.title: Masters of the Bay
event.text: From Martaban to Malacca, Bengali merchantmen and warships now command the sea lanes of the Bay of Bengal. Our textiles are exchanged for Moluccan spices at Malacca, while Burmese teak and rubies flow through Martaban into Bengali markets. This is the greatest maritime commercial network since the days of Srivijaya. But the question remains: shall we enforce our dominance through naval power, projecting force across the ocean, or channel this wealth into building a trading civilization without peer?

options.text: Command the seas with Bengali warships.

modifiers.name: Maritime Dominion
modifiers.text: Bengali warships enforce commercial supremacy across the Bay of Bengal, building a naval tradition that extends the reach of Bengal's merchantmen to ever more distant shores.

options.text: Build the greatest emporium the world has seen.

modifiers.name: Entrepot Wealth
modifiers.text: Bengal's ports serve as the central hub of Indian Ocean commerce. The prestige of our trading houses endures, and war-torn provinces recover quickly under the umbrella of Bengali trade.

destiny.name: Woven Air
destiny.text: Bengal's muslin, so fine it was called 'woven air', becomes the foundation of a global textile monopoly. Secure the Malabar coast, dominate cotton and silk markets, and establish Bengal as the world's premier cloth exporter.

conditions.text: Own Kozhikode, or a subject owns it
A market the country is in

children.text: Cotton is produced in the market
Cotton is traded in the market

event.title: Woven Air
event.text: They call it 'woven air', muslin so fine a bolt can pass through a ring. Bengal's cloth monopoly is now unassailable. From the Malabar ports to the markets of the Levant, no textile competes with ours. European merchants call Dhaka 'the Manchester of the East,' though we were first by centuries. This is the apex of the weaver's art, and the foundation of an empire built not on conquest but on craft. Shall we press our advantage through exclusive control of the cotton supply, or open our ports to all comers and grow rich on volume?

options.text: Control the supply of cloth to the world.

modifiers.name: Cloth Monopoly
modifiers.text: Bengal's unassailable dominance of the global textile trade assimilates diverse populations into a unified Bengali identity, lending the dynasty legitimacy and the loyalty of subject peoples.

options.text: Let our ports become the crossroads of trade.

modifiers.name: Ocean Emporium
modifiers.text: Bengal's open-port policy transforms its cities into the greatest trading centers in Asia, earning diplomatic leverage and intelligence networks, though the focus on commerce comes at some cost to military readiness.

destiny.name: Conquest of Bihar
destiny.text: Secure Bengal's western flank by conquering Bihar, the heartland of the Ganges plain. Patna and Darbhanga command the great river's middle reaches and provide the strategic depth Bengal needs to project power westward.

conditions.text: Own Patna, or a subject owns it
Own Darbhanga, or a subject owns it

event.title: The Conquest of Bihar
event.text: Bengali armies have swept across the Ganges plain and planted their banners in Patna and Darbhanga. Bihar (the land of the ancient Magadha kingdom, the cradle of Buddhism) now answers to Bengal. With these conquests, the sultanate secures the strategic middle Ganges and gains access to Bihar's rich agricultural hinterland. The road westward lies open.

options.text: Bihar is ours. The Ganges awaits.

destiny.name: Campaign of the Ganges
destiny.text: Push the boundaries of Bengali power south into Orissa at Cuttack and west along the Ganges to the sacred city of Varanasi. This establishes Bengal as the dominant power of eastern India.

conditions.text: Own Kataka, or a subject owns it
Own Varanasi, or a subject owns it

event.title: Campaign of the Ganges
event.text: The campaign has been a triumph. Cuttack, capital of the Gajapati kings, has fallen, bringing all of Orissa under Bengali suzerainty. To the west, the sacred ghats of Varanasi now fly Bengali colors. From Orissa's Jagannath temple to the burning grounds of Kashi, Bengal's power extends across the breadth of eastern India. But the army is far from home. How shall we consolidate these vast new territories, through military logistics that sustain our campaign forces, or through the administrative order that turns occupation into governance?

options.text: Ensure our supply lines hold for the next push.

modifiers.name: River Supremacy
modifiers.text: Bengal's mastery of riverine logistics allows armies to reinforce and campaign far along the Ganges, fielding larger forces than the enemy expects.

options.text: Establish order in the conquered provinces.

modifiers.name: Occupation Order
modifiers.text: Efficient administration of conquered territories transforms military occupation into lasting governance, with mercenary garrisons enforcing order while cheaper war declarations push the frontier ever outward.

destiny.name: Empire of the Ganges
destiny.text: The ultimate expression of Bengali military power: an empire stretching from the delta to the Mughal heartland. Take Agra, Lucknow, and the sacred temple of Puri. Bengal rules the Ganges from source to sea.

conditions.text: Own Agra, or a subject owns it
Own Lucknow, or a subject owns it
Own Puri, or a subject owns it

event.title: Empire of the Ganges
event.text: It is done. The Mughal capitals at Agra and Lucknow answer to Bengal. The temple of Lord Jagannath at Puri is under our protection. From the Hooghly to the Yamuna, from Orissa to Awadh, the Ganges and all its tributaries flow through Bengali territory. This is an empire to rival any in Indian history, built from the delta outward, defying every expectation that Bengal would remain a provincial backwater. Shall this empire rest on the might of its levies and the terror of its armies, or on the calculated application of force that secures victory before battle begins?

options.text: Raise the greatest armies the subcontinent has seen.

modifiers.name: Imperial Authority
modifiers.text: Bengal's imperial cavalry and fortified garrisons project power across the conquered Gangetic plain, though maintaining this vast military apparatus strains the treasury.

options.text: Victory belongs to those who prepare.

modifiers.name: Conqueror's Legacy
modifiers.text: Bengal's armies loot the wealth of conquered lands, recruit seasoned regiments at speed, and deploy devastating artillery: the enduring legacy of a realm forged through conquest.

units.name: Bengali River Galley
units.text: A shallow-draft oared vessel designed for the narrow, winding channels of the Ganges delta. Fast and maneuverable, these galleys patrol the waterways that serve as Bengal's highways.

units.name: War Boatman
units.text: Riverine infantry who fight from boats and on muddy shorelines. During the monsoon season when cavalry is useless, these paik-backed warriors are Bengal's primary fighting force.

units.name: Bengal Patrol Boat
units.text: A swift vessel designed to protect Bengal's river and coastal trade routes from pirates and smugglers. Lighter and faster than standard warships, patrol boats are the workhorses of Bengal's commercial security.

units.name: Chittagong Trader
units.text: A deep trading ship built in the yards of Chittagong for the yearly run across the bay to Malacca and Pasai. It carries more than other ships of its size and sails slower, and its presence is felt in the sea lanes it works.

units.name: Banduqchi
units.text: Bengali matchlock musketeers who form the gunpowder infantry of the Sultanate and later the Nawab's armies. Their disciplined volley fire is devastating in the open terrain of the Bengal plains.

units.name: Banduqchi Militia
units.text: Levy musketeers drawn from Bengal's soldier and peasant communities, armed with matchlocks and trained in basic volley tactics.

units.name: Bengali Sepoy
units.text: Professional musket infantry of the Nawab era, trained in European drill and equipped with flintlock muskets. The Bengali sepoy combines subcontinental martial tradition with modern military discipline.

buildings.name: Delta Bund
buildings.text: Earthen embankments and flood control systems that protect Bengal's rice paddies from the annual monsoon floods, and the winter wheat sown on the same fields once the waters drain. These bunds channel floodwaters into irrigation canals, turning a destructive force into agricultural abundance.

children.text: The location's raw material is Rice
The location's raw material is Wheat

buildings.name: Jute Works
buildings.text: Retting pools, stripping sheds and gunny looms beside a delta river. Bundles of jute lie in the slow water until the fibre comes away from the stalk, and it is then dried, spun and woven into sacking. It can be built only on a river.

buildings.name: Muslin Workshop
buildings.text: A specialized weaving shed where Bengali craftsmen produce the world's finest cotton cloth. The muslin of Dhaka and Sonargaon is so sheer that bolts of it can pass through a finger ring.

buildings.name: Arong
buildings.text: A Bengali textile marketplace where muslin and other fine cloth is traded. The greatest arong at Panam Nagar in Sonargaon draws merchants from across Asia, making it one of the subcontinent's premier commercial centers.

buildings.name: Jami Mosque
buildings.text: A grand congregational mosque built in Bengal's distinctive brick-and-terracotta tradition, with curved chala roofs and intricate floral carvings that blend Islamic architecture with indigenous Bengali forms.

buildings.name: Customs House
buildings.text: A port revenue office that regulates Bengal's overseas trade. Customs officers assess duties on incoming and outgoing cargoes, channeling the wealth of the Bay of Bengal trade into the state treasury.

buildings.name: Arsenal
buildings.text: A weapons manufactory and military depot producing firearms, gunpowder, and ammunition. Bengal is one of the world's largest producers of saltpetre, the critical ingredient in gunpowder.

buildings.name: Sarraf Kothhi
buildings.text: A Nawab-era banking house where Bengali financiers manage credit, exchange currencies, and finance long-distance trade. These institutions make Bengal a financial center rivaling any in the Mughal Empire.

buildings.name: Indigo Vat
buildings.text: A works of steeping and beating vats where the cut indigo is soaked, fermented and pressed into dye cakes, so that the land yields more of its blue for the textile industries of Europe.

where.text: The location's raw material is Dyes

buildings.name: Golden Muslin House
buildings.text: The pinnacle of Bengal's textile industry, a palatial workshop and trading hall where the finest muslin and silk are produced, displayed, and sold to merchants from across the known world.

buildings.name: Victory Pillar
buildings.text: A monumental stone column commemorating Bengal's conquests along the Ganges, serving as both a garrison strongpoint and a symbol of martial prowess that inspires troops and overawes the conquered.

list.name: Diwan-i-Bangala
list.text: The Bengal revenue diwan, originally a Mughal subah bureau under Akbar's settlement of 1582 and comprehensively reorganised by Murshid Quli Khan after he became diwan in 1700 and moved his capital from Dhaka to Murshidabad in 1717. He cleared the arrears of the great zamindars, settled the kharaj directly with thousands of smaller holders, and remitted the imperial khalisa share to Delhi for two decades before the diwan's accounts became a Bengali institution in their own right. The bureau's books fixed the revenue of every taluk, every parganah, every ferry, and every fishing weir in the wettest, richest, most populous province of the Mughal world.

list.name: Talukdari Zamindari
list.text: The layered Bengali land-tenure system in which the throne collected its revenue not directly but through hereditary zamindars who held tenures of sometimes vast extent and farmed them in turn to talukdars and minor intermediaries. By the late seventeenth century the great zamindars of Burdwan, Rajshahi, Dinajpur, Birbhum, and Nadia commanded resources, walled seats, and armed retainers rivalling small kingdoms; Rajshahi alone paid more revenue than several Deccan subahs combined. Their cooperation kept the realm running, and their resistance ended Nawabs.

list.name: Faujdari Thanas
list.text: The Mughal-era network of faujdars, military-judicial officers posted to thanas across the subah, charged with policing the grand trunk roads of Bengal, suppressing dacoity in the riverine country, and putting down the chronic banditry of the Naga and Bhuyan zones in the eastern hills. Each faujdar held a small standing fauj of horse and matchlockmen and exercised concurrent magisterial powers over criminal cases. The system gave the throne reach into districts the diwan's revenue clerks could not by themselves hold, and the faujdar's seal stood at the seam between the Mughal peace and the dacoit's blade.

list.name: Jagat Seth Treasury
list.text: The alliance between the Nawab and the Marwari banking dynasty of Manikchand and his nephew Fatehchand, whom Emperor Muhammad Shah formally titled Jagat Seth, the Banker of the World. From the 1720s the family held the contract on the Murshidabad mint, brokered the remittance of revenue to Delhi via hundi networks reaching from Surat to Patna, and underwrote the Nawabate's short-term finance against the next harvest. By the 1750s Robert Orme called Jagat Seth the greatest shroff and banker in the known world; his withdrawal of confidence from Siraj ud-Daulah in 1757 made the English coup at Plassey possible.

list.name: Hussain Shahi Patronage
list.text: The syncretic court culture of the Hussain Shahi sultans (1493-1538) at Gaur, whose chancery patronised Bengali Vaishnava poetry alongside Persian and Arabic letters, sponsored translations of the Mahabharata into Bengali by Maladhar Basu and Kavindra Parameshvara, employed the future Vaishnava saint Sanatana Goswami as a court secretary before his renunciation, and built mosques in distinctively Bengali brick idioms drawing on local Hindu temple craft. The arrangement rooted the sultanate in the rural Hindu population and the landed gentry, but offended orthodox ulama who looked outside Bengal for authority.

list.name: Naib Nazim of the East
list.text: The deputy-governorship of eastern Bengal seated at the old Mughal capital of Sonargaon and later Dhaka, the senior of three subordinate nizamats (the others being Bihar and Orissa) under the Nawab. The Naib Nazim ruled the great delta with a free hand, holding his own court, his own treasury, and his own faujdars; in practice the post was an apanage that the Nawab gifted to a son or a powerful kinsman, and it institutionalised the structural tension between the river-port east and the Murshidabad capital. When Sarfaraz Khan held it under Shuja-ud-Din the eastern revenues flowed; when he didn't, they didn't.

list.name: Subahdari Chancery
list.text: The Persianate secretariat of the Bengal subah, staffed by munshi scribes drawn from the Hindu Kayastha and Khatri castes alongside Mughal-trained Muslim secretaries. The chancery handled diplomatic correspondence with Delhi and the imperial farmans that authorised every major act of the Nawabate, the drafting of sanads for the European factories at Hugli, Chinsura, Chandernagore, and Calcutta, and the trilingual record-keeping in Persian, Bengali, and Arabic that bound the subah to the empire and to the world trade beyond it. From the chancery's quills came the very treaties that, by 1765, turned Bengal's revenues over to a foreign company.
